metaTitle: Best Flat Top Grills in 2026, Reviewed
metaDescription: Flat top gas grills compared on plate steel, zones and cooking area, from a tabletop convertible to a 44 inch cart rig with six burners.
expertTake: The Royal Gourmet GB4000P is the best all-round flat top here because it pairs a roughly 35 inch plate with a hard cover and four burners you can run separately. The ROVSUN 4 burner foldable is the value pick if you want wheels and a fold-flat stand for the least money. Skip the whole category if you mostly cook burgers and steaks for two, because a flat top has no grate marks and no fat drip-off and a plain grill does that job better.
introParagraphs: A flat top grill is a gas burner box with a solid steel plate on top instead of grates. Everything cooks in its own fat on that plate, which is why it excels at smash burgers, fried rice, breakfast and anything small enough to fall through a grate.

The plate is the part you are really buying. How thick it is, how many burners sit under it and how well it sheds grease decide whether the machine cooks evenly in year one and still looks usable in year three.

products.name: Royal Gourmet GB4000P 4-Burner Flat Top, 35 Inch
products.description:
The GB4000P is built around a wide plate over four separate burners, so you can leave one end screaming hot for a smash burger and keep the other end warm for buns or eggs. The listing quotes a cooking area of 766, which puts it at the roomy end of the freestanding group and well past the 389 of the PD4001 from the same maker.

The trade is footprint and weight. At roughly 35 inches wide plus folding shelves, it wants a dedicated corner of the patio and a cart you do not move daily. The hard cover is a real asset here: it keeps rain and dew off the bare plate between cooks, which is where most rust starts.

Ownership is the usual flat top routine of scrape, wipe, oil and close the lid. Plan on a separate soft cover if the unit lives outside through a wet winter, and keep a spare propane cylinder, because four burners drain a standard 20 pound tank faster than a two burner tabletop does. For a family that cooks breakfast and dinner on the same plate, this is the most balanced machine in the lineup.
products.bestFor: Families who want a full size cart griddle with a lid and real zone control.
pros: Four burners give genuine multi-zone control
Hard cover protects the plate between cooks
Large plate feeds a full table at once
Folding side tables with tool hooks save space
cons: Needs a permanent spot and a heavy cart
Four burners empty a propane tank quickly
Bare steel still needs oiling after every cook

products.name: Royal Gourmet GB6000 6-Burner Flat Top, 44 Inch
products.description:
The GB6000 is the largest machine here: six burners across roughly 44 inches. Its distinguishing feature is a ceramic coated plate, which the listing describes as scratch and rust resistant, so it skips the long seasoning ritual that bare steel demands. That coating is the reason it suits owners who dread rust more than they love patina.

Coated plates are a compromise. They need less oil and wipe clean, but metal spatulas can chip a coating, and a chipped patch exposes steel that then behaves like any bare plate. Against the 35 inch GB4000P, the extra width buys capacity for a large party rather than better searing, since heat per burner is the same idea in a longer box.

The cost of the width is logistics. A 44 inch cart will not fit most garage corners or a hatchback, and it burns propane in proportion to its six burners. Buy it only if you regularly cook for ten or more, otherwise the wide plate mostly stays cold and idle.
products.bestFor: Large households and party hosts who want a coated plate and maximum width.
pros: Six burners across a very wide plate
Ceramic coating cuts the seasoning chore
Two side tables with knife holder and towel rack
Plate wipes clean with little oil
cons: Too wide for small patios and car trunks
Metal tools can chip the coating
Six burners burn through propane fast

products.name: Royal Gourmet PD4001 4-Burner Flat Top with Hood
products.description:
The PD4001 splits into a cart-mounted griddle and a tabletop unit, which is the one trick the larger machines cannot do. Four burners share 34,000 BTU over 389 square inches, a gentle ratio that leans toward even cooking rather than raw flame.

Because the plate is smaller than the GB4000P, you lose the ability to keep a lot of food warm on a cool zone. You gain a machine that can ride in an SUV to a tailgate, then sit on a cart at home. The black hood shields the plate from the elements and keeps debris off it between uses.

The weak spot of convertible designs is the joint between cart and body, which needs checking for wobble each time you reassemble it. Pick this over the ROVSUN foldable if you want a hood and a more traditional griddle build, and over the GB4000P if you value moving it more than feeding a crowd.
products.bestFor: Owners who tailgate sometimes and still want a proper cart at home.

Gentle burner ratio for even plate heat
Hood keeps the steel clean
Four independent burners for zone cooking
cons: Smallest plate of the cart models here

products.name: ROVSUN 4-Burner Foldable Flat Top with Wheels and Lid
products.description:
ROVSUN gives the cheapest route to four separate burners on a rolling frame. The listing states each burner at 10,000 BTU, 40,000 in all, and the scissor legs fold flat so the whole thing stores against a garage wall.

That convenience is paid for in rigidity. Scissor legs flex more than a welded cart, so a heavy plate full of food will wobble more than it does on the GB4000P. The listing also mentions an enameled tray and an electronic ignition, which are small comforts that save fumbling with a lighter.

It is the sensible first flat top for someone unsure the category will stick. If you do keep using it, inspect the leg pivots and wheel bolts each season, because folding hardware loosens with repeated setup. Compared with the 4 burner ROVSUN stand-alone listing, the foldable version trades some stiffness for packability.
products.bestFor: First time buyers who need wheels, a lid and a fold-flat frame.
pros: Folds flat for garage or trunk storage
Four independent burners at 10,000 BTU each
Wheels make it easy to roll out
Lid and enameled tray are included
cons: Scissor legs flex under a loaded plate
Folding hardware loosens with frequent setup

products.name: Dephet 4-Burner Flat Top with Detachable Stand, 40,000 BTU
products.description:
Dephet pairs four burners with a plate the listing calls heavy duty cast iron, plus a stand that detaches so the top can be used on a table. The cooking area figure in the listing is 455, which sits between the PD4001 and the GB4000P in raw size.

A cast iron plate holds heat well once hot but is slow to respond when you turn the dial down. It also demands careful seasoning and dry storage, since cast iron rusts quickly if left damp. Treat the claimed 40,000 BTU as a ceiling, not a promise of searing, and judge it by how the plate behaves after a few cooks.

This is the pick for a shopper who wants four zones and a detachable stand at the lowest outlay and accepts a lesser known brand. Check that replacement burners and knobs can be bought separately before you commit, because parts availability is the usual weakness of lower profile makers.
products.bestFor: Budget shoppers who want four zones and a detachable stand.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A flat top lives or dies on its plate. Cold-rolled carbon steel in the 4 mm to 6 mm range spreads heat edge to edge and holds a seasoning layer, while thinner plates warp when frozen patties hit a hot surface. Many buyers never ask the thickness at all and compare burner counts instead. Few listings here state thickness at all, so treat any plate not described as heavy duty or thick steel as light until proven otherwise.

Zones let you sear on one end and hold at a simmer on the other, which is the real reason to buy a multi-burner flat top. Count how many burners you can run separately, not how many knobs exist. The GB4000P and PD4001 both offer four, the GB6000 six, but only the width of the plate decides how useful the extra zones are.

Advertised width is not cooking area. A 36 inch class plate is around 720 square inches and a 28 inch class plate around 500 to 520. In this lineup the PD4001 lists 389 square inches and the GB4000P lists 766, nearly double, so a similar looking four burner machine can feed twice the people.

A rear grease chute with a large cup is far easier to live with than a small centre hole. Flat tops run all fat off one drain, so a poor design clogs mid-cook. Check where the cup sits, because a cup tucked behind a stand leg is a chore to empty.

Bare cold-rolled steel is not non-stick until seasoned and rusts quickly if left wet. Coated plates like the ceramic coated GB6000 need less oil and resist rust, but they give up the patina and can chip. Pick coated if you cook infrequently, bare steel if you cook weekly.

A hard cover or hood protects the plate between cooks and adds steaming and melting ability, but it raises stored height and is not a substitute for a weatherproof cover. The GB4000P ships with a hard cover and the PD4001 with a hood, while the Dephet and ROVSUN rely on lids or covers that suit short term protection.

specDecoder.meaning: It is the sum of every burner's rated output, not a measure of how hot the plate gets. A thick plate on a low BTU box often cooks better than a thin plate on a high one.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Dephet and ROVSUN quote 40,000 BTU, yet the PD4001 cooks at 34,000 BTU over a different area.

specDecoder.meaning: Square inches of the plate you can actually load. It is smaller than width times depth because of the grease channel and edge lip.
specDecoder.watchFor: The GB4000P's 766 is a listing figure; compare it with the PD4001's 389 rather than reading the inch label.

specDecoder.meaning: Cold-rolled steel, cast iron or a coated finish. It sets how fast the plate heats, how it holds heat and how it rusts.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Dephet's cast iron cools slowly, the GB6000's ceramic coating can chip.

specDecoder.meaning: The number of separate flame sources under the plate. More burners mean more zones, but only if each has its own valve.
specDecoder.watchFor: The ROVSUN lists four independent burners; confirm the same on any unit with a single shared knob.

specDecoder.meaning: The size of the stored unit versus the working unit. It decides whether the machine is portable or a fixture.
specDecoder.watchFor: The ROVSUN folds flat; the GB6000 does not and needs a permanent spot.

howWeEvaluated.title: Plate and burner build
howWeEvaluated.description: We read each listing for plate material, burner count and how the heat is distributed. Machines that disclose plate material or thickness scored higher than those that only quote BTU. Hot rolled, cast iron and ceramic coated plates were judged on their own tradeoffs rather than ranked blindly.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cooking area versus footprint
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated cooking area to overall width and flagged mismatches. The 766 of the GB4000P versus the 389 of the PD4001 showed how similar looking cart griddles can differ in usable space. Smaller plates were not penalised if they were honest about it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership cost
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed rust risk, seasoning effort, cover protection and parts supply. Hoods and hard covers earned credit, as did coated plates for low maintenance owners. Unclear parts support from lesser known brands counted against a pick.

howWeEvaluated.title: Portability and storage
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked folding stands, wheels and removable carts, since a griddle that cannot be stored or moved tends to go unused. The ROVSUN foldable and the PD4001 convertible scored well here, the GB6000 less so.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for recurring themes such as wobbling frames, chipped coatings and slow cooling rather than any score. The patterns informed the cons lists, not the ranking alone.

cards.label: Bare or cast iron
cards.text: Builds a real seasoning layer and shrugs off metal tools, but rusts if left wet and needs oil after every cook. The Dephet cast iron and the steel plates of the GB4000P and PD4001 fall here.

cards.label: Coated
cards.text: The ceramic coated GB6000 wipes clean with little oil and resists rust, yet a chip exposes bare steel and metal spatulas risk that.

howToChoose.note: Weekly cooks should pick bare steel and a lid like the GB4000P. Occasional cooks who fear rust should pick the GB6000.

rows: Fixed width and cart, maximum capacity

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A hard cover or hood that closes over the whole plate, plus a coating or a plan to oil the plate after each cook. Rust, not burner failure, is what retires outdoor griddles.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The GB4000P's hard cover and the PD4001's hood protect best, and the GB6000's coating covers the rest. A soft cover still goes over any of them.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You cook for a crowd weekly and want the GB4000P or GB6000, where width and a protective cover save you from rust and crowding.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You cook mainly for two and only occasionally. The Dephet or ROVSUN delivers four zones without the footprint, while the PD4001 splits the difference.

maintenance.why: Food stuck to a cooled plate turns into carbon that is hard to remove. A flat scraper on a hot plate lifts residue in seconds.
Oil is the barrier between steel and moisture in the air. Skipping it is how flash rust forms overnight.
A full cup overflows onto the cart or the patio. Check it before you light the burners.

maintenance.interval: Every few months, or after rust
maintenance.why: Heat several thin layers of oil until the plate darkens. This rebuilds the non-stick finish that scraping wears away.
Brush soapy water over the regulator and hose joints and look for bubbles. Replace anything that leaks before the first cook of the year.

faq.q: Is a flat top better than a regular grill?
faq.a: They do different jobs. A flat top excels at smash burgers, eggs, fried rice and small items, but it gives no grate marks and traps fat in the cook, so steaks and chicken taste different than over open flame.

faq.q: Do I need to season a flat top?
faq.a: Bare steel and cast iron plates do. Coated plates like the ceramic coated GB6000 need less, though a thin oil coat after cooking still helps all of them.

faq.q: How wide a flat top should I buy?
faq.a: Compare measured square inches, not advertised width. About 400 square inches feeds a small family, while the GB4000P's listed 766 serves a crowd.

faq.q: Can I use a flat top on a balcony?
faq.a: Propane is the most restricted fuel for balconies in many cities and leases. Check fire code and your lease before buying any propane flat top.
Bare steel left wet or unoiled rusts quickly, and rust is the most common reason outdoor griddles are replaced. A hard cover, thin oil coat after each cook and a dry storage spot prevent it.

faq.q: Does more BTU mean better searing?
faq.a: Not on its own. Plate thickness and zone control matter more, and a high BTU box with a thin plate warps and heats unevenly.
